title: Risk assessment and risk management
blurb: Use risk tools the way current guidance intends, respond to hazards, and tell positive risk management apart from risk aversion.
question: Mrs Patel, 81, has capacity and wants to walk to the toilet on her own at night, although she had a fall at home last month. Her daughter asks the nurse to keep the bed rails up. What is the most appropriate approach?

teach.body: A hazard is anything with the potential to cause harm, such as a wet floor or a faulty hoist. Risk is the chance that harm happens and how serious it would be. Risk management means identifying hazards, judging the risk, putting proportionate controls in place, recording them and reviewing them. In plain English: spot it, judge it, control it, write it down, check it again. Nurses must act without delay on risks to safety (Code standard 16) and reduce the likelihood of mistakes and harm (Code 19.1).

steps.label: Identify
steps.sub: hazards and who could be harmed

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.sub: likelihood and severity, with the person

teach.h: Contemporary tools support judgement; they do not replace it
teach.body: Validated tools structure an assessment: NEWS2 for deterioration, a pressure ulcer scale such as Braden or Waterlow, MUST for malnutrition, VTE risk assessment. But NICE is explicit that some tools must not be used to predict outcomes. Falls: do not use falls risk prediction tools; offer a comprehensive falls assessment instead (NG249, 2025). Self-harm: do not use risk scales to predict suicide or decide who is treated or discharged (NG225, 2022).

teach.caption: A low score never cancels a nurse's clinical concern; escalate if worried.
Proficiency P6.10 asks nurses to understand this difference.

teach.body: A person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because it is unwise (Mental Capacity Act 2005 s1(4)). If someone with capacity chooses an activity with some risk, the nurse explains the risks, agrees controls with them, respects their choice and records the discussion. Restricting them for staff reassurance is risk aversion and may breach their rights.

teach.h: Responding to a hazard you discover

children.label: Interim controls + escalate to manager for the risk register

teach.h: Worked scenario: Mrs Patel on a care of older people ward
teach.body: Mrs Patel, 81, has capacity and wants to walk to the toilet alone at night. Staff Nurse Dee does not use a falls prediction score; she starts a comprehensive falls assessment (lying and standing BP, medicines, vision, continence). She talks with Mrs Patel and her daughter about the risks of bed rails and of falling, and they agree a plan: low bed, frame and call bell within reach, night light, non-slip footwear and a toileting check before sleep. Dee records the decision and reviews it daily.

teach.text: A score is not a decision. NG249 says do not use falls risk prediction tools, and NG225 says do not use risk scales to decide discharge after self-harm. A low NEWS2 does not override your concern either.

items: Identify, evaluate, control, record, review; reassess whenever the person's condition changes.
Tools support clinical judgement; NG249 and NG225 rule out prediction tools for falls and suicide.
Risk management balances harms and benefits with the person; risk aversion restricts to remove all risk.
Unwise is not the same as lacking capacity: agree controls and record the discussion.
Make immediate hazards safe; escalate persistent risks so they reach the risk register.

summary: You can now carry out and review a risk assessment, use contemporary tools in the way current NICE guidance intends, and respond to hazards proportionately. You can also distinguish positive risk management from risk aversion and support people with capacity to take informed risks.

A.q: Edna, 84, is admitted to a medical ward after a urinary infection. A student asks which falls risk score to complete. What is the most appropriate reply?
options: Complete a falls prediction score within 24 hours
Use a score if she has fallen in the last year
Wait until Edna has a fall before assessing
Offer Edna a comprehensive falls assessment
A.why: NICE NG249 (2025) advises not using falls risk prediction tools and offering all hospital inpatients aged 65 and over a comprehensive falls assessment and management.

whyNot.0: NG249 advises against falls prediction tools, whatever the timing.
whyNot.1: A previous fall does not make prediction tools appropriate; a full assessment is offered.
whyNot.2: Assessment is offered to all inpatients aged 65 and over, before any fall.

A.q: Mr Hughes had a low pressure ulcer risk score on admission. Two days later he has a stroke and cannot reposition himself. What should the nurse do?
options: Keep the admission plan until the weekly review
Refer him to tissue viability if a sore develops
Reassess his pressure ulcer risk now and update plans
Repeat the same risk score at the next routine handover
A.why: NICE CG179 advises reassessing pressure ulcer risk when clinical status changes. Loss of ability to reposition is a major new risk factor, so prevention must be updated now.

whyNot.0: Waiting for a weekly review leaves a high-risk person on a low-risk plan.
whyNot.1: Prevention aims to stop damage, not respond once it has occurred.
whyNot.3: His status has already changed; reassessment should happen now, not at handover.

A.q: A nurse notices fluid spreading across the corridor outside a bay where patients are walking. What should she do first?
options: Make the area safe with a sign and arrange cleaning
Complete an incident report on the system
Tell the domestic team at the end of the shift
Ask all the patients to stay in their bays all afternoon
A.why: Code standard 16 requires acting without delay on risks to safety, and HASAWA s7 requires reasonable care for others. Removing the immediate hazard comes first; reporting follows.

whyNot.1: Reporting matters, but the immediate slip hazard must be controlled first.
whyNot.2: Delaying until the end of the shift leaves the hazard in place.
whyNot.3: Confining patients is disproportionate when the hazard can be removed.

B.q: Which statement best describes the difference between risk management and risk aversion?
options: Risk management removes all hazards; risk aversion accepts some
Risk aversion uses validated tools; risk management does not
Risk aversion is required by law for people over 65
Risk management weighs harms and benefits with the person
B.why: Risk management weighs harms against benefits with the person and puts proportionate controls in place so valued activity continues. Risk aversion tries to avoid any chance of harm, often at the cost of independence (proficiency P6.10).

whyNot.0: This reverses the two: aversion seeks to remove risk, management accepts managed risk.
whyNot.1: Both may involve tools; the difference is how harms and benefits are balanced.
whyNot.2: No law requires risk aversion for older people; the MCA protects their right to decide.

B.q: Mr Ellis, 79, has capacity and wants to walk to the day room with his frame although he is unsteady. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Ask him to use a wheelchair from now until he is discharged
Agree a supervised walking plan with him and record it
Seek his son's consent before he walks unaided
Complete a best interests decision about walking
B.why: Positive risk management agrees proportionate controls with the person so they can do what matters to them. He has capacity, so his choice is respected (MCA 2005 s1(4)) and the discussion is documented.

whyNot.0: Removing activity is risk aversion and risks deconditioning.
whyNot.2: An adult with capacity makes his own decisions; his son cannot consent for him.
whyNot.3: Best interests decisions apply only where capacity is lacking, which is not the case here.

B.q: Leah, 19, attended after self-harm. A colleague says her risk scale score is low, so she can be discharged without further assessment. What does NICE NG225 advise?
options: Discharge her, as the low score supports it
Repeat the scale in 4 hours, then decide
Admit her, as all self-harm needs a hospital admission
Assess her needs and agree a safety plan with her
B.why: NICE NG225 (2022): do not use risk tools and scales to predict suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to decide who is offered treatment or discharged. Use a psychosocial assessment of needs and a safety plan agreed with the person.

whyNot.0: NG225 says risk scales must not decide discharge.
whyNot.1: Repeating the scale still relies on a tool NG225 says not to use for this decision.
whyNot.2: Care is based on assessed needs, not blanket admission.

C.q: The keypad lock on a dementia ward's exit door has failed twice this month. Estates say a new system needs funding. What should the nurse in charge do?
options: Report each failure on the incident system and wait for estates
Lock the door with a key and keep the key at the nurses' station
Put interim measures in place and escalate it for the risk register
Move all the patients with dementia to another ward until it is fixed
C.why: A persistent risk that cannot be fixed at ward level needs interim controls now and escalation so it is formally assessed, owned and recorded on the risk register (P6.3; Code 16.1, 25.1).

whyNot.0: Reporting alone, without interim measures or escalation, leaves an ongoing risk unmanaged.
whyNot.1: Locking a ward door restricts all patients' liberty and creates a fire safety risk; it is not a proportionate control.
whyNot.3: Moving every patient is disproportionate and causes harm through relocation.

C.q: Mr Adeyemi, 66, has a NEWS2 score of 2. His wife says he is 'not himself' and the nurse thinks he looks greyer than earlier. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Repeat observations in 12 hours as the score is low
Act on the concern: increase monitoring and inform the doctor
Reassure his wife that a score of 2 is within the normal range today
Wait until the score reaches 5 before escalating
C.why: NEWS2 supports, and does not replace, clinical judgement. For scores of 1 to 4 the registered nurse decides on monitoring frequency and escalation, and concern from family is an important signal (RCP 2017; Martha's Rule).

whyNot.0: Twelve-hourly is the minimum for a score of 0, and it ignores clear clinical concern.
whyNot.2: False reassurance dismisses a family concern that should prompt review.
whyNot.3: Clinical concern justifies escalation at any score.

C.q: Mrs Rowe is on room air with SpO2 91% (NEWS2 Scale 1). Her other observations score 0. Which response does NEWS2 require?
options: Observe at least hourly and inform the medical team
Repeat observations in 4 to 6 hours
Continuous monitoring and an urgent critical care referral
No change, as her total score is below 5
C.why: SpO2 91% or less scores 3 on Scale 1. A score of 3 in any single parameter needs a minimum of hourly observations and the registered nurse informs the medical team (NEWS2, RCP 2017, Charts 1 and 4).

whyNot.1: Four to six hourly applies to a total of 1 to 4 without a single parameter scoring 3.
whyNot.2: Continuous monitoring and critical care referral apply at a total of 7 or more.
whyNot.3: A single parameter scoring 3 triggers a response whatever the total.

reteach.title: Seatbelts, not locked garages
reteach.question: If driving is risky, do we ban cars or add seatbelts? How does that apply to patients?

blocks.h: Manage the risk, keep the life
blocks.body: Banning a risky activity removes the risk but also the benefit. Positive risk management is like a seatbelt: the person keeps doing what matters, with controls that make serious harm less likely. Tools such as NEWS2 or a pressure ulcer scale are like a dashboard warning light: useful, but you still look out of the window. And if the light says all is fine but you smell smoke, you stop the car.

blocks.h: Positive risk management in five moves

blocks.text: Restricting someone with capacity 'for their own safety' is risk aversion, not good practice. An unwise choice is not a lack of capacity (MCA s1(4)).

explain.body: Risk assessment identifies hazards, judges likelihood and severity, sets controls and records them. It must be reviewed when the person's condition or situation changes, not just on a fixed date.

test.q: When should a person's VTE risk be reassessed after the admission assessment?
options: Every 72 hours in all adult inpatients, whatever their condition
Once a week on the ward's audit day
At consultant review or if their condition changes
Before discharge and not before
test.why: NICE NG89: assess VTE and bleeding risk on admission and reassess at the consultant review or if the clinical condition changes.

whyNot.0: NG89 links reassessment to consultant review and clinical change, not a fixed 72-hour cycle.
whyNot.1: A weekly audit day is unrelated to the person's changing risk.
whyNot.3: Waiting until discharge would miss changes during the stay.

explain.body: Use validated tools to structure assessment and clinical judgement to interpret them. Do not use falls risk prediction tools (NG249) or self-harm risk scales to predict suicide or decide treatment (NG225).

test.q: Which statement about falls risk tools reflects NICE NG249 (2025)?
options: Use them for all patients over 65
Do not use them to predict falls risk
Use them to predict a person's risk of falling
Use them weekly and after each fall
test.why: NG249 advises not to use falls risk prediction tools; instead offer comprehensive falls assessment to people who meet the criteria, including all inpatients aged 65 and over.

whyNot.0: Inpatients over 65 are offered a full assessment, not a prediction tool.
whyNot.2: Prediction is exactly what NG249 advises against.
whyNot.3: Repeating an unsupported tool does not make it valid.

explain.body: When a person with capacity wants to do something risky, explain the risks, agree controls together, respect their decision and record it. Unwise does not mean lacking capacity (MCA s1(4)).

test.q: A man with capacity chooses to keep smoking outside the hospital entrance despite advice. Which principle applies?
options: He lacks capacity because the choice he makes is unwise
Staff should stop him going outside the ward
His family can decide on his behalf
His decision is respected though it may be unwise
test.why: MCA 2005 s1(4): a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because it is unwise. Staff can give advice, but respect his choice.

whyNot.0: An unwise decision alone does not show a lack of capacity.
whyNot.1: Preventing an adult with capacity from leaving the ward is an unlawful restriction.
whyNot.2: Relatives cannot make decisions for an adult who has capacity.

explain.body: Make immediate hazards safe straight away, then report. Risks that cannot be solved locally are escalated so they are assessed, owned and recorded on the organisation's risk register, with interim controls meanwhile.

test.q: Several call bells in one bay have been faulty for weeks despite repeated reports. What is the best next step for the nurse?
options: Give hand bells and escalate to the ward manager
Report it again and wait for the repair
Move the bay's patients to the corridor
Ask the relatives to stay overnight to keep watch on them
test.why: Interim controls (hand bells, more frequent checks) reduce the risk now, and escalation to the manager ensures the persistent risk is formally assessed and recorded on the risk register (P6.3; Code 16.1).

whyNot.1: Repeated reporting without escalation has not worked and leaves the risk unmanaged.
whyNot.2: Moving patients to a corridor creates new risks to safety and dignity.
whyNot.3: Relatives are not responsible for providing safe care on the ward.
